text: Every successful product starts with an idea.
But having a good idea and knowing whether it's worth building
are two very different things.
Before committing resources, product teams need to understand
their customers, evaluate competitors, identify risks, and
challenge their assumptions. That can take days, and important
questions can still go unanswered.
What if this process could be more structured, and more
evidence-driven?
That's the problem I'm working on with ProductLens AI, a product
research and decision-support platform I'm building for product
managers, founders, and business analysts.
It will take a product idea or a proposed feature and turn it
into a structured assessment:
competitors, customer pain points, potential failure scenarios,
and ways to validate it. The goal isn't to replace product
managers. It's to help them make better-informed decisions
before investing time and money in building.
Several tools already help with parts of this.
General-purpose AI assistants like ChatGPT and Claude can help
brainstorm and analyze product ideas.
Perplexity answers questions with cited sources.
And Productboard helps teams centralize customer feedback and
align on priorities. Each one covers a valuable part of the
product management process.
But connecting these activities into one structured assessment
still takes a lot of manual work.
ProductLens AI explores whether research, competitive analysis,
failure analysis, and validation planning can be combined into
one coordinated workflow: one that questions assumptions, links
claims to evidence, and turns risks into measurable experiments.
Whether that actually produces better results is something I'll
test as part of the project.
Here's how it's designed to work.
A user enters a product idea, its audience, and some business
context. For example: an AI-powered personal finance app for
international students in the United States.
ProductLens AI will define the research scope and hand it to a
team of specialized AI agents, each responsible for one part of
the analysis.
It starts by collecting information from public sources:
official product websites, documentation, customer reviews, and
industry publications. An orchestrator then coordinates three
specialized agents. The Market and Competition Agent examines
existing solutions and room for differentiation.
The Customer and Adoption Agent looks at user needs, pain
points, and barriers to adoption.
The Failure and Risk Agent works out how the product could fail,
which assumptions are critical, and how to reduce those risks.
Each agent has its own system prompt, a defined role, and a
structured output format, so one large research problem becomes
several focused tasks.
A convincing AI answer isn't necessarily an accurate one.
So ProductLens AI adds a dedicated evaluation stage.
An Evaluator Agent reviews the findings for unsupported claims,
inconsistencies, missing evidence, and recommendations too vague
to act on. When it finds an issue, that finding is revised and
checked again. And every claim is labelled either supported by
evidence, or a hypothesis that still needs validation, so
uncertainty becomes an explicit part of the result.
The proposed application uses a modern web stack, large language
models, structured prompts, and an orchestration layer that
manages each stage. Building it needs model API access, token
credits, research access, and somewhere to run it.
Those are still being confirmed.
Token use, cost, and processing time will be tracked throughout.
The final deliverable is a Product Decision Brief:
competitive insights, customer pain points, ranked failure
risks, recommended experiments, and measurable success criteria,
each linked to its evidence.
To find out whether ProductLens AI actually adds value, I'll
test it on ten standardized product scenarios from different
industries, each run three ways.
A: a single-prompt baseline. B:
the multi-agent workflow without the evaluator.
And C: the complete ProductLens workflow, with evaluation and
revision. The model, the inputs, and the evidence stay the same,
so I can see whether specialization and self-evaluation make a
measurable difference.
I'll measure several things. Factual grounding:
are claims actually supported by their cited sources?
Relevance: are the risks and customer problems specific to this
product? Actionability: can the recommended experiments really
be run and measured? I'll also plant deliberate errors to see
whether the evaluator catches them, and check that the
structured outputs are valid.
Finally, I'll compare token use, response time, and cost per
report, to see what the extra complexity costs.
The project succeeds if the complete workflow consistently
produces more grounded, relevant, and actionable assessments
than the baseline, at an acceptable cost.
If the extra agents and evaluation don't make a meaningful
difference, or cost too much, that's an important finding too.
The goal isn't to prove that a multi-agent system works.
It's to find out whether it's worth using.
With ProductLens AI, I'm exploring how prompt engineering and
agentic AI can move beyond generating content to support real
product decisions. Because building the right product starts
with understanding the right problems, questioning our
assumptions, and validating before we build.
